item.title: Your First Home to stimulate development but more help needed
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government's new "Your First Home" scheme has been broadly welcomed by property experts as a positive step for first-time buyers, though industry voices caution that deeper supply-side reforms may be needed to truly address the UK's housing challenges.

Support for first-time buyers

The initiative aims to stimulate housing development by making homeownership more accessible, particularly for younger buyers struggling to save substantial deposits. Through a combination of discounted pricing and shared ownership options, the scheme could help thousands take their first step onto the property ladder.

Mortgage advisors note that the programme builds upon existing schemes like Help to Buy, but with some key differences:

  • More flexible eligibility criteria compared to previous initiatives
  • Potential for lower deposit requirements in certain developments
  • Options for shared equity with local authorities

Persistent supply challenges

While welcoming the demand-side support, housing analysts highlight that fundamental supply constraints continue to limit overall market accessibility. The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) suggests that without addressing planning bottlenecks and construction sector capacity, price pressures may persist even with increased first-time buyer support.

Key supply-side issues that could benefit from further attention include:

  • Streamlining the planning application process
  • Incentives for brownfield site development
  • Investment in construction skills training

For prospective homeowners, the current landscape suggests that while government schemes can provide valuable assistance, exploring all available mortgage products and seeking independent financial advice remain important steps in the homebuying journey.

item.title: Two-thirds of landlords will increase rents if taxes rise
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

A recent study has revealed that a significant proportion of landlords in the UK may raise rents if faced with increased taxation or additional costs. The findings suggest that potential tax changes could lead to higher rental prices, with landlords becoming more selective about their tenants in response to financial pressures.

Impact of Tax Changes on Rental Prices

The research highlights that nearly two-thirds of landlords would consider increasing rents to offset any rise in taxes or operational costs. This could have a direct impact on tenants, particularly those already struggling with affordability in the current rental market. Whilst landlords aim to maintain profitability, tenants may face added financial strain as a result.

For homeowners and investors, this underscores the importance of staying informed about potential tax reforms and their implications. Understanding how these changes might affect rental income and property management costs could help landlords prepare for future adjustments.

Selective Tenant Choices

In addition to raising rents, the study suggests that landlords might become more selective when choosing tenants. This could mean prioritising applicants with stable incomes, strong credit histories, or longer rental commitments. Whilst this approach may help landlords mitigate financial risks, it could also make it more challenging for some tenants to secure rental properties.

For tenants, this highlights the value of maintaining a solid financial profile and ensuring all necessary documentation is readily available when applying for rentals. Landlords, on the other hand, may wish to review their tenant selection criteria to balance financial security with fairness.

What Does This Mean for the Rental Market?

The potential for higher rents and stricter tenant selection could reshape the UK rental market. Tenants may need to budget more carefully, whilst landlords might explore strategies to manage costs without passing the full burden onto renters. Proactive communication between landlords and tenants could also play a key role in navigating these changes.

Ultimately, the findings serve as a reminder of the interconnected nature of taxation, property investment, and rental affordability. Both landlords and tenants may benefit from staying informed and seeking professional advice where necessary to adapt to evolving market conditions.

As the UK property market continues to evolve, understanding the potential impact of tax changes on rental prices and tenant selection remains crucial for all parties involved.

item.title: £170k renovation vs new build cost
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Homeowners considering whether to renovate an older property or purchase a new build may find recent research revealing the financial implications of both options particularly insightful. The study highlights how bringing period homes up to modern standards could cost upwards of £170,000 – a figure that warrants careful consideration against the price of a newly constructed property.

The true cost of upgrading older homes

Research indicates that comprehensive renovations to match contemporary living standards often involve substantial investment. Common upgrades include improving energy efficiency through better insulation, replacing outdated heating systems with modern alternatives, and updating electrical wiring to current safety regulations. Structural repairs, damp proofing, and replacing single-glazed windows with double or triple glazing can also contribute significantly to costs.

While period properties often boast desirable character features, many require extensive modernisation to meet today's expectations of comfort and functionality. The £170,000 figure represents a full-scale refurbishment rather than cosmetic improvements, highlighting how seemingly minor issues can accumulate into major expenses when updating older buildings.

New builds versus renovation projects

For buyers weighing their options, new build properties typically come with modern specifications as standard, including energy-efficient appliances, contemporary heating systems, and warranties that cover structural defects. These benefits might prove attractive compared to the unpredictable costs and timescales associated with major renovation work.

However, period properties often occupy more established locations and offer architectural charm that new developments might lack. Some homeowners might prefer investing in renovation projects to create their ideal home while preserving historical character, despite the potentially higher initial outlay.

Prospective buyers may wish to consider not just the purchase price, but the total cost of ownership when comparing properties. Mortgage options for renovation projects differ from standard purchase mortgages, with some lenders offering specialist products for substantial refurbishments.

Ultimately, the decision between renovation and new build depends on individual priorities, budget considerations, and appetite for project management. While new builds offer convenience, older properties provide unique opportunities to create bespoke living spaces – provided purchasers are prepared for the potential scale of investment required.

item.title: Clear roadmap required for landlord energy investment
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
Industry Calls for Clarity on Landlord Energy Efficiency Rules

By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Property industry leaders are urging the government to provide clear guidance on upcoming energy efficiency requirements for private rentals. The National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) and Energy Saving Trust have jointly called for a detailed roadmap outlining timelines and expectations for landlords.

The Push for Transparent Timelines

With proposed regulations likely to require significant property upgrades, landlord groups argue that clarity is essential for effective planning. Currently, proposals suggest all new tenancies should meet minimum energy efficiency standards (EPC band C) by 2025, extending to all existing tenancies by 2028.

Industry bodies highlight that without firm deadlines and detailed requirements, landlords may struggle to:

  • Budget for necessary improvements
  • Schedule works around tenancies
  • Access appropriate funding schemes
  • Understand which upgrades will comply

Balancing Environmental and Practical Concerns

While supporting the environmental objectives behind energy efficiency reforms, property experts stress the need for realistic implementation. Many rental properties, particularly older buildings, may require substantial retrofitting to meet proposed standards.

Landlords considering energy improvements might benefit from reviewing current government grant schemes and tax relief options. The lack of clear guidance about future requirements, however, makes long-term planning challenging for property investors.

The NRLA suggests that a phased approach with adequate notice periods could help landlords prepare while maintaining rental supply. They emphasise that sudden, poorly communicated changes might lead to some landlords exiting the market, potentially reducing available housing.

As the consultation process continues, industry watchers anticipate further details about exemptions, enforcement and financial support mechanisms. For now, landlords may wish to monitor developments while considering gradual improvements to their properties' energy performance.

item.title: 35 CSS graduates qualify in 2026
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Chartered Surveyors Society (CSS) has celebrated the qualification of 35 new chartered surveyors in 2026, with six professionals completing their training this autumn. This latest cohort brings the total number of graduates from the CSS Academy to its highest annual figure since the programme's inception.

Growing Talent in the Property Sector

The property industry continues to see strong demand for qualified surveyors across residential, commercial and valuation specialisms. The CSS Academy's structured training programme combines practical experience with professional development, preparing graduates for the challenges of modern property assessment and valuation work.

Industry observers note that the consistent output of newly qualified surveyors helps address skills shortages in certain regions, particularly for residential valuation work. The profession remains attractive to those seeking a career combining technical expertise with client-facing responsibilities in the property market.

Pathways to Professional Qualification

Becoming a chartered surveyor typically requires:

  • A relevant degree or conversion course
  • Completion of the Assessment of Professional Competence (APC)
  • Two years of structured training under supervision
  • Specialisation in a chosen survey discipline

The CSS Academy provides structured support throughout this process, with many trainees coming through graduate schemes at major surveying practices. Successful candidates qualify as members of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS), the profession's governing body.

For homeowners and property investors, working with RICS-qualified surveyors can provide assurance of professional standards when dealing with valuations, structural surveys or building defect assessments. The growth in qualified professionals may help maintain service levels as demand for property expertise continues across the UK market.

item.title: The Market Has Moved – Investors Have Shifted To Using Brokers More In 2026
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK property finance market in 2026 has undergone significant changes, with fragmentation, stricter credit policies, and fluctuating lender appetites reshaping the landscape. Investors who once relied on direct relationships with lenders are now increasingly turning to specialist brokers to navigate this complex environment. This shift highlights the growing importance of brokers in securing competitive mortgage deals and tailored financial solutions.

The Changing Landscape of Property Finance

The property finance market has become increasingly fragmented, with lenders adopting tighter credit policies and frequently adjusting their criteria. This volatility has made it challenging for investors to secure favourable terms without expert guidance. In response, many are now recognising the value of working with brokers who have access to a wide range of lenders and can provide bespoke advice based on individual circumstances.

Specialist brokers have evolved from being a convenience to a necessity, offering insights into market trends and helping investors identify opportunities that might otherwise be overlooked. Their expertise has become particularly crucial in a market where lender appetites can change rapidly, and competition for the best deals is fierce.

The Role of Brokers in 2026

Brokers are playing a pivotal role in helping investors navigate the complexities of the property finance market. With their in-depth knowledge of lender criteria and access to exclusive deals, they can save investors time and potentially significant sums of money. For those considering expanding their property portfolios or refinancing existing assets, brokers offer a streamlined approach to securing the most suitable finance options.

Additionally, brokers can provide tailored advice on how to meet lenders’ stricter requirements, such as improving credit scores or restructuring financial profiles. This personalised support has become invaluable in a market where even small missteps can lead to missed opportunities or unfavourable terms.

As the property finance market continues to evolve, brokers are likely to remain a vital resource for investors seeking to maximise their returns and minimise risks. Their ability to adapt to changing market conditions and provide strategic guidance ensures they remain at the forefront of property finance solutions.

For investors navigating the complexities of the UK property market in 2026, partnering with a specialist broker could prove to be a wise decision. With their expertise and access to a diverse range of lenders, brokers are well-positioned to help investors achieve their financial goals in an increasingly challenging environment.

item.title: Leaseholders warn PM: ‘Words must now become law’
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Leasehold campaigners have cautiously welcomed the prime minister’s pledge to introduce leasehold reform legislation before Christmas, though many homeowners remain sceptical after years of delays. Speaking at the Labour Party Conference, Andy Burnham promised "long overdue" changes to protect leaseholders from unfair practices, declaring an end to exploitative charges.

Key reforms in the pipeline

The draft Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, published earlier this year, contains several significant proposals for England and Wales:

  • Making commonhold the default tenure for most new flats
  • Capping ground rents to prevent excessive charges
  • Replacing leasehold forfeiture with a fairer enforcement system
  • Introducing independent regulation of property agents

The government has confirmed that property agents would need appropriate qualifications and licences to operate, with a regulator empowered to withdraw licences where standards fall short. These changes aim to address what campaigners describe as "one of Britain’s biggest consumer scandals".

Cautious welcome from campaigners

The National Leasehold Campaign (NLC) has acknowledged the progress while stressing the need for swift action. Katie Kendrick, NLC co-founder, noted that whilst the prime minister’s personal commitment matters, leaseholders have endured "years of consultations and missed deadlines".

Many homeowners had hoped for a firmer commitment to abolish leasehold entirely in favour of commonhold – a system where residents collectively own their building. The current proposals stop short of this, focusing instead on reforming rather than replacing the existing system.

Kendrick emphasised: "Leasehold remains fundamentally flawed. Millions still face excessive charges and lack control over their homes despite technically owning them." The government previously stated its intention to end leasehold during this Parliament, but campaigners await concrete legislation.

Questions remain over regulation

The proposed property agent regulator has drawn particular scrutiny from campaigners. The NLC insists any regulator must be:

  • Genuinely independent from industry interests
  • Properly funded to enforce standards effectively
  • Empowered with meaningful sanctions

Kendrick warned against "industry self-regulation dressed as reform", stressing that leaseholders shouldn’t bear the costs of regulating managing agents. The NLC argues that agents themselves should fund the regulator rather than passing costs to homeowners through service charges.

As the government prepares to introduce its bill, all eyes will be on Westminster to see whether these long-promised reforms finally materialise. For millions of leaseholders, the test will be whether the legislation delivers meaningful change or falls short of expectations once again.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK property market is witnessing notable developments as estate agencies expand their reach and adapt their models to cater to evolving homeowner needs. From new self-employed agent initiatives to regional network growth, these changes could offer fresh opportunities for those looking to buy or sell property.

Rogers Stewart Introduces Self-Employed Agent Model

Rogers Stewart, a prominent estate agency franchise partner, has recently launched a self-employed ‘Personal Agent’ operation in Teesside. This innovative model aims to provide a more personalised and flexible service to homeowners. Steve McDonald, a seasoned estate agent with over three decades of experience, has been appointed to lead this initiative. McDonald, who previously managed Rogers Stewart’s Stockton branch, will operate across Norton, Wynyard, Billingham, and Sedgefield under the Reeds Rains brand.

McDonald emphasised the benefits of the Personal Agent model, stating that it allows him to serve as the sole point of contact for clients throughout the entire property transaction process. From initial market appraisals to negotiation and completion, homeowners can rely on his expertise and guidance. His goal is not to become the largest local estate agent but to earn the trust and recommendations of his clients.

Paul Rogers, head of Rogers Stewart, expressed his support for McDonald’s new venture, highlighting his significant contributions to Reeds Rains over the years. The agency operates eight Reeds Rains branches and one Your Move branch across the North East and Yorkshire, providing a strong foundation for this expansion.

Moveli Enhances South West Presence

Meanwhile, Moveli, a growing estate agency, has strengthened its South West network with the appointment of Emily Hall in Exeter. With over 14 years of experience in the property and sales sector, Hall brings extensive knowledge of the Exeter and Devon markets to her new role. Her career includes tenures at Winkworth, Burgoynes, and Martin & Co, making her a valuable addition to Moveli’s team.

At Moveli, Hall will focus on residential sales across Exeter and its surrounding areas. Ben Littlewood, co-founder and co-CEO of Moveli, praised her expertise and expressed enthusiasm about her joining the company. He noted that the South West is a key growth area for Moveli, and Hall’s appointment aligns with their strategy to expand their presence in this region.

These developments reflect the dynamic nature of the UK property market, with estate agencies introducing innovative models and strengthening their regional networks. Homeowners and buyers in these areas might find these changes beneficial, offering more tailored services and local expertise.

As the property market continues to evolve, keeping an eye on such developments could help individuals make informed decisions when navigating their property journeys.

item.title: Planning approvals for new homes plunge to 14-year low
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Recent data has revealed a concerning decline in planning approvals for new homes across England, reaching their lowest quarterly level in over a decade. According to the latest Housing Pipeline report from the Home Builders Federation (HBF), based on Glenigan data, just 45,315 homes received planning permission in the second quarter of 2026. This marks a 21% drop compared to the previous quarter and reflects a broader trend of shrinking housing supply.

Over the 12 months to June 2026, local authorities granted permission for 214,515 homes, the lowest annual figure since 2013. This represents an 8% year-on-year decrease and is 36% below the peak recorded in 2017. The decline has been particularly stark for larger developments, with approvals for sites containing more than 10 properties falling by 21% quarter-on-quarter and 14% compared to the same period last year.

Private Housing Approvals Hit Record Lows

The figures also highlight a sharp reduction in private housing approvals, which fell by 19% compared to the previous quarter and 15% year-on-year. Additionally, only 1,234 projects involving three or more homes secured approval during the second quarter of 2026—the lowest quarterly figure on record. Over the past 12 months, just 5,783 such projects were approved, another record low. Smaller developments, consisting of one or two homes, accounted for roughly half of all approved projects.

Government Initiatives Aim to Boost Demand

item.title: Landlords warn Budget tax hikes could push rents higher
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords across the UK are expressing growing concerns about potential tax changes in the upcoming Budget, with many warning that increased costs could lead to higher rents for tenants. Recent research highlights that 64% of landlords are considering raising rents to offset financial pressures, whilst 88% are worried about a proposed two percentage point increase in income tax rates on rental income from personally owned properties. These findings come ahead of the Budget announcement on 28 October and follow a series of regulatory changes affecting the private rented sector.

Potential Impact on Tenants

With rising costs and regulatory changes, landlords may pass on additional expenses to tenants in the form of higher rents. According to Pegasus Insight’s Tenant Trends research, over a quarter of renters already expect landlords to increase rents to comply with the Renters’ Rights Act, which came into effect in England on 1 May. The Act introduced significant reforms, including the abolition of Section 21 evictions and the introduction of assured periodic tenancies. Whilst these changes aim to provide greater security for tenants, they have also increased operational costs for landlords.

Furthermore, Pegasus Insight’s Landlord Trends research suggests that 83% of landlords are becoming more selective when choosing tenants in response to tax and regulatory pressures. This could lead to reduced choice for renters and fewer properties available on the market, potentially exacerbating the challenges faced by tenants in an already competitive rental sector.

Concerns Over Court Delays

Another pressing issue for landlords is the potential for court delays under the new possession regime. The Renters’ Rights Act requires landlords to use statutory possession grounds if tenants do not leave after a valid notice expires. However, 91% of landlords are reportedly ‘very concerned’ about court backlogs, which could delay the recovery of their properties. Mark Long, founder and director of Pegasus Insight, emphasised the importance of a reliable court system, stating that ensuring its capacity to cope with increased demands should be a priority for policymakers.

Long also highlighted the need for stability in the private rented sector. “Landlords are already adapting to significant changes under the Renters’ Rights Act, and the prospect of further tax increases in the Budget is adding to the uncertainty,” he said. “Additional costs could influence landlord behaviour in ways that ultimately affect tenants through higher rents, reduced choice, or fewer homes available to rent.”

As the Budget approaches, landlords and tenants alike are keenly awaiting details of potential tax changes. With rising costs and regulatory pressures, the private rented sector faces a period of adjustment. Ensuring a balance between landlord responsibilities and tenant protections will be crucial in maintaining a fair and sustainable rental market.

item.title: Sub-5% mortgage deals vanish as major lenders raise rates
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Mortgage rates continue their upward trajectory as major lenders withdraw sub-5% deals, leaving prospective buyers and remortgagers with fewer affordable options. Nationwide, Virgin Money and TSB have all recently increased their rates, following a broader market trend that has seen borrowing costs rise steadily since early 2024.

The shrinking pool of sub-5% mortgages

Where borrowers could access rates below 4% earlier this year, the current market offers significantly fewer competitive deals. The lowest five-year fixed remortgage rate now stands at 5.02% with NatWest, while Virgin Money's equivalent two-year product starts at 5.01%.

A handful of lenders still maintain limited sub-5% products, though these typically require substantial deposits. Yorkshire Building Society currently offers a two-year fix at 4.93% (with a £1,495 fee), while Skipton provides a five-year option at 4.91% (with a £1,995 fee). For those with a 20% deposit, rates now typically begin around 5.08%.

Mortgage experts suggest the situation may worsen before it improves. Aaron Strutt of Trinity Financial notes: "We're reaching a point where sub-5% fixed deals are becoming scarce, though some competitive tracker mortgages remain available. Further rate rises from lenders seem likely in the current climate."

Impact on monthly repayments

The rate increases translate to substantially higher monthly payments for borrowers. On a typical £400,000 mortgage over 25 years, monthly repayments at 3.5% would be approximately £2,003. At the current average of 5.01%, this rises to £2,341 - an extra £338 each month, or over £4,000 annually.

This affordability squeeze coincides with weakening housing market activity. Recent Bank of England data shows mortgage approvals for house purchases have fallen to their lowest level since December 2023, suggesting many potential buyers are pausing their plans amid the challenging financial climate.

For homeowners approaching the end of their current deal, mortgage advisers might recommend reviewing options well in advance. Those with sufficient equity could consider securing one of the remaining competitive fixed rates, while others may explore tracker mortgages as a potentially more flexible alternative during this period of volatility.

item.title: House price growth stalls as flat prices fall for 15th month in a row
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK housing market continues to show signs of cooling, with annual price growth slowing to 0.8% - the lowest level recorded in over two years. According to Zoopla's latest House Price Index, the average property now costs £273,000, with analysts predicting further softening to around 0.5% growth by year-end.

Mortgage costs dampen market activity

Higher borrowing costs appear to be the primary factor influencing current market conditions. With average mortgage rates reaching 5.2% - their highest point in three years - monthly repayments have risen by approximately £150 compared to early 2026 levels. This increase has contributed to a 9% annual decline in agreed sales, whilst available property stock has grown by 5%.

Homebuyers now find themselves in a stronger negotiating position, with the supply-demand balance particularly shifting in London and southern England where available stock has risen by 8%. The West Midlands has experienced the most significant drop in sales (down 15%), followed by the East of England (14% decrease). Scotland's market remains comparatively resilient, with just a 1% sales decline and 3% more properties available.

Changing dynamics between property types

The market slowdown has highlighted growing differences between houses and flats. Flat prices have now fallen for fifteen consecutive months, decreasing by 1.3% annually, whilst house prices have maintained a 1.3% increase nationwide. Regional variations remain pronounced, with Northern Ireland leading growth at 6.7%, followed by the North West (3.6%) and Scotland (3.3%).

Market conditions have prompted many sellers to reconsider their pricing strategies. Around 25% of properties newly listed in September had previously been on the market within the past year, with 60% of these relisted at lower asking prices. This trend is especially noticeable among flats and larger houses, which typically take longer to sell. In London, where a third of flats coming to market are relisted, sellers appear particularly willing to adjust expectations.

With properties taking longer to sell across most regions - only half of northern England homes and three in ten London properties find buyers within three months - homeowners considering a sale may wish to research local market conditions thoroughly. The current climate suggests realistic pricing and flexibility could be increasingly important factors for successful transactions in the coming months.

item.title: Mortgage approvals slump to lowest level since 2023 as buyers sit on sidelines
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Mortgage approvals for house purchases in the UK have dropped to their lowest level since December 2023, according to the latest data from the Bank of England. The figures reveal a steady decline in buyer activity, with August marking the fourth consecutive month where approvals fell below 60,000. Experts suggest this downturn reflects growing affordability pressures and a cautious approach from potential homebuyers.

Mortgage approvals dip amid rising costs

The Bank of England reported 54,900 mortgage approvals in August, down from 55,900 in July. This figure is notably lower than the six-month average of approximately 60,100, indicating a slowdown in housing market activity. The effective interest rate on newly drawn mortgages also rose from 4.45% in July to 4.6% in August, adding to the financial challenges faced by buyers.

Richard Donnell, executive director at Zoopla, highlighted the impact of higher mortgage costs on buyer behaviour. He noted that average mortgage rates have increased significantly since the start of the year, rising from 4% to over 5%. This has led many buyers to delay purchasing decisions, with some opting to wait for more favourable conditions or inject additional equity to secure their desired property.

Remortgaging activity also declines

Remortgage approvals with a different lender also saw a decline in August, dropping from 34,600 in July to 34,000. This suggests that despite many borrowers reaching the end of their fixed-term rates, refinancing demand has softened. Katie Clinton, head of financial services advisory at KPMG UK, attributed this trend to ongoing affordability pressures and broader economic uncertainty.

Nathan Emerson, CEO of Propertymark, echoed these concerns, pointing to global unrest and its impact on consumer confidence. He noted that while the housing market has faced significant challenges this year, there remains a cautious optimism as buyers and sellers navigate the evolving landscape.

What next for the housing market?

The Bank of England’s decision to maintain the base rate at 3.75% in September reflects a balancing act between controlling inflation and supporting economic stability. However, with mortgage rates remaining elevated and affordability pressures persisting, the housing market is likely to face continued headwinds in the coming months.

For those considering entering the market, it could be worth exploring options such as longer mortgage terms or higher deposits to mitigate rising costs. Meanwhile, homeowners approaching the end of their fixed-term rates may wish to seek advice on remortgaging options to secure competitive deals amidst fluctuating interest rates.

As the market adjusts to these challenges, staying informed and seeking professional guidance could help buyers and homeowners make well-informed decisions in an increasingly complex environment.

item.title: Valuation appointment can make or break an instruction, sellers say
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

For homeowners looking to sell their property, the valuation appointment with an estate agent can be a pivotal moment. Recent research highlights just how much this meeting influences their decision on which agent to instruct. According to a survey by GetAgent, 86% of sellers consider the valuation appointment important, with nearly half (47%) describing it as very important. This underscores the significance of making a strong first impression during this crucial interaction.

The Importance of Valuation Reports

The survey, which gathered insights from UK homeowners who sold their properties in the past year, revealed that the quality and presentation of a valuation report play a significant role in securing an instruction. Nearly six in 10 respondents (59%) stated that the report’s quality influenced their choice of estate agent. Furthermore, 69% said that a professionally presented report would boost their confidence in an agent’s abilities.

Consistency also emerged as a key factor. A majority of sellers (81%) felt that an agency appeared more professional when its valuation report, website, marketing materials, and communications shared consistent branding. This suggests that attention to detail and a cohesive approach can leave a lasting positive impression on potential clients.

Speed and Follow-Up Matter

Timeliness is another critical factor for sellers. Over half (51%) expect to receive their valuation report within 24 hours of the appointment. This highlights the importance of swift follow-up, as delays could potentially harm an agent’s chances of winning the instruction.

Colby Short, co-founder and CEO of GetAgent, emphasised the broader implications of the valuation appointment. He noted that sellers are not just evaluating the proposed valuation figure but also assessing the agent’s knowledge of the local market, their understanding of the property, and their marketing strategy. The entire experience, from the initial meeting to the follow-up, shapes the seller’s decision.

For estate agents, the message is clear: securing an instruction goes beyond simply getting through the door. The valuation appointment, the quality of follow-up materials, and the speed of response all contribute to winning the trust and confidence of sellers.

Ultimately, homeowners may wish to consider these factors when choosing an estate agent, ensuring they work with a professional who not only provides a competitive valuation but also delivers a seamless and consistent experience.

item.title: Surge in CCJs puts landlords on alert over tenant referencing
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords across England and Wales are increasingly prioritising tenant referencing amidst a rising number of County Court Judgments (CCJs) and regulatory changes in the private rental sector. According to recent research, nearly one million consumer CCJs were registered in 2025, marking an 11.8% increase from the previous year. This heightened focus on referencing comes as new rules under the Renters’ Rights Act have reshaped the rental landscape, prompting landlords to reassess their tenant selection processes.

The impact of regulatory changes

The Renters’ Rights Act, which came into effect in May 2025, introduced significant changes for landlords and tenants. One of the key provisions limits advance rent payments to no more than one month’s rent for most new tenancies. Additionally, Section 21 ‘no-fault’ evictions have been abolished in England. These changes have shifted the dynamics of the rental market, with landlords placing greater emphasis on tenant affordability and referencing to mitigate financial risks.

Research from Leaders’ Summer 2026 Lettings Report highlights this trend, with 45.2% of landlords stating that referencing has become more important since the new rules were introduced. Among respondents, 37.4% considered referencing significantly more critical, while 7.8% viewed it as slightly more important. However, 41.7% of landlords rely on their letting agents to handle the referencing process entirely.

Key factors in tenant selection

When choosing tenants, landlords appear to prioritise employment status and income above other factors. The survey found that 40.6% of landlords identified these as the most important criteria, while 38.8% relied on referencing reports provided by their letting agents. Previous landlord references, credit history, and personal judgement ranked lower in importance.

Despite the heightened focus on referencing, the majority of tenants appear to pass these checks without issues. According to the survey, 82% of tenants reported no problems during the referencing process. For those who did encounter difficulties, income (4%), employment type (2.2%), and credit history (1.6%) were the most common reasons. Interestingly, 36.8% of tenants believed rigorous referencing benefits both landlords and tenants equally, while 21% felt it primarily favours landlords but also offers some protection to tenants.

Balancing landlord and tenant interests

The evolving rental market underscores the need for a balanced approach to tenant referencing. With advance rent payments now limited, referencing has become a critical tool for landlords to assess financial reliability. However, it is equally important to ensure that the process remains fair and accessible for tenants.

Allison Thompson, chief lettings officer at Leaders, noted, “With advance rent no longer available, referencing has moved from being one tool among many to being the cornerstone of tenant selection. It is essential for landlords to strike a balance between protecting their investments and offering tenants a fair chance to secure rental properties.”

As the rental market continues to adapt to regulatory changes and economic pressures, tenant referencing remains a key factor in maintaining stability and trust between landlords and tenants. Landlords may wish to review their referencing processes to ensure they are both thorough and equitable, while tenants might consider preparing financial documentation in advance to streamline applications.

By Bambang Setiawan

In recent years, residential property investors have navigated a challenging landscape marked by tax adjustments, rental reforms, and rising borrowing costs. Amidst these changes, some are turning their attention to a less conventional investment opportunity: mixed-use properties, particularly those combining a shop on the ground floor with flats above. While these properties can offer dual income streams from a single asset, they also present unique challenges when it comes to securing financing.

What Are Mixed-Use Properties?

Mixed-use properties are buildings that serve both residential and commercial purposes. A common example is a high street shop with residential flats above. These properties can be appealing to investors seeking diversification, as they generate rental income from both tenants and business occupiers. However, their hybrid nature means they fall into a distinct category when it comes to mortgages, often requiring specialised lending solutions.

Challenges with Mortgage Applications

Securing a mortgage for a mixed-use property can be more complex than obtaining financing for a purely residential or commercial property. Many high street lenders are hesitant to finance these assets due to their dual-purpose nature, which can make them harder to value and sell if the borrower defaults. Additionally, lenders may perceive mixed-use properties as higher risk, particularly if the commercial element relies on a specific tenant or business type.

For investors considering this route, it could be worth exploring specialist lenders or mortgage brokers who have experience with mixed-use properties. These professionals may offer more tailored solutions and a deeper understanding of the unique risks and rewards associated with such investments.

Benefits of Mixed-Use Investments

Despite the challenges, mixed-use properties can offer several advantages. The combination of residential and commercial tenants can provide a steady income stream, potentially reducing reliance on a single source of rental revenue. Furthermore, these properties often benefit from prime high street locations, which can enhance their long-term value and appeal.

For those willing to navigate the complexities of financing and management, mixed-use properties could represent a strategic addition to a diversified property portfolio. However, thorough due diligence is essential, particularly in assessing the viability of the commercial element and understanding the specific lending criteria for these assets.

As with any property investment, seeking professional advice and carefully evaluating the risks and rewards can help ensure a sound decision. Mixed-use properties may not be suitable for everyone, but for the right investor, they could unlock unique opportunities in the UK property market.

item.title: The Overlooked Repairs That Become an Investor’s Most Expensive Problems
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Many buy-to-let landlords discover too late that small maintenance issues can snowball into costly repairs if left unattended. What begins as a minor leak or superficial crack often develops into structural damage requiring extensive work - potentially disrupting tenancies and eroding rental yields significantly.

Common Minor Issues That Escalate

Property investors might be surprised how seemingly trivial problems can become serious over time. Some frequently overlooked concerns include:

  • Dripping taps or small water leaks that gradually damage flooring and subfloor structures
  • Worn window seals allowing moisture penetration and potential timber rot
  • Minor cracks in walls or ceilings that may indicate foundation movement
  • Sticking doors or windows suggesting frame warping or subsidence
  • Guttering blockages leading to water ingress and exterior deterioration

Why Preventative Maintenance Pays Off

Whilst immediate repairs might appear an unnecessary expense, proactive maintenance typically proves far more economical than emergency fixes. Landlords may wish to consider:

  • Scheduling biannual property inspections between tenancies
  • Budgeting 1-2% of the property value annually for maintenance
  • Promptly addressing tenant reports of minor issues
  • Building relationships with reliable local tradespeople
  • Keeping detailed records of all works completed

A stitch in time doesn't just save nine in property maintenance - it could potentially save thousands of pounds in avoidable damage whilst maintaining the asset value and rental potential. Savvy investors recognise that proactive care forms part of responsible portfolio management.

item.title: ‘Christmas comes early’ for housebuilders as shares surge on buyer scheme
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK government’s announcement of a new first-time buyer scheme has sparked a significant surge in housebuilder shares, offering a potential boost to the property market. Named ‘Your First Home’, the initiative aims to help eligible buyers in England purchase new-build properties with deposits as low as 2.5%. The scheme includes a government-backed equity loan of up to 20% of the property’s value, alongside an initial interest-free period. Full details, including income limits and local price caps, are expected to be unveiled at next month’s Budget.

How the Scheme Could Impact Housebuilders

The proposed scheme has already had a positive effect on the stock market, with shares in major housebuilders rising sharply. Companies such as Persimmon, Barratt Redrow, and Taylor Wimpey saw gains of around 12-15%, whilst Crest Nicholson and Vistry also experienced notable increases. Building materials firms, including Ibstock and Marshalls, joined the rally, with their shares climbing by 21% and 12% respectively.

Analysts suggest that developers with a strong focus on open-market sales, particularly in the south and south-east of England, are likely to benefit the most from the initiative. Conversely, firms with less exposure to these markets or properties priced above the scheme’s proposed caps may see relatively slower growth. Anthony Codling, managing director at RBC Capital Markets, described the announcement as a “big catalyst” for the sector, noting that it has effectively brought “Christmas early” for UK housebuilders.

Potential Benefits for First-Time Buyers

The primary goal of ‘Your First Home’ is to reduce the deposit barrier faced by first-time buyers, making homeownership more accessible. By offering a 20% equity loan and an initial interest-free period, the scheme could significantly lower upfront costs. This approach mirrors elements of the former Help to Buy equity loan programme, though final terms are yet to be confirmed.

The introduction of income limits and local property price caps is expected to ensure that the scheme targets those who need it most. For buyers, this could mean greater affordability in areas where property prices have historically been prohibitive. Additionally, the focus on new-build homes may help stimulate demand in this sector, supporting both buyers and developers.

Market Reaction and Future Outlook

The announcement comes at a time when housebuilders are grappling with weaker buyer confidence and rising construction costs. The potential boost from ‘Your First Home’ could provide much-needed relief, particularly for firms heavily reliant on new-build sales. Investors appear optimistic, with the sharp rise in housebuilder shares reflecting confidence in the scheme’s potential to rejuvenate the market.

Whilst further details, including implementation timelines and costs, are expected in the Budget, the initial response suggests that the initiative could be a game-changer for both buyers and the property sector. Borrowers considering their options may wish to keep an eye on developments as the scheme takes shape.

As the government prepares to finalise the details of ‘Your First Home’, the property market awaits what could be a transformative initiative for first-time buyers and housebuilders alike. With the Budget just weeks away, stakeholders are keen to see how the scheme will be rolled out and what it could mean for the future of homeownership in the UK.

item.title: Landlord exodus: More than 500 rental homes leaving PRS every day
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent analysis by property data firm TwentyEA reveals a significant trend in the UK’s private rented sector (PRS), with an estimated 505 rental homes exiting the market daily in 2026. This marks a sharp increase compared to 2020, where the rate was less than a third of current levels. The findings highlight ongoing challenges for landlords, driven by a combination of regulatory changes, taxation pressures, and rising costs.

The Impact of Regulatory Reforms

The Renters’ Rights Act, which came into effect in England on 1 May, has introduced sweeping changes to the rental landscape. Key reforms include the abolition of Section 21 evictions, the introduction of a new tenancy system, and restrictions on rental bidding. Whilst these measures aim to improve tenant protections, they have coincided with a surge in landlord sales. In 2024, around 111,696 rental properties left the PRS, a figure that rose to approximately 181,000 in 2025. Although there were initial signs of a slowdown in landlord exits earlier this year, the trend appears to have regained momentum.

It’s worth noting that TwentyEA’s analysis does not directly attribute the rise in landlord sales to the Renters’ Rights Act. Instead, the firm points to broader pressures on landlord returns, including taxation, mortgage costs, and upcoming energy-efficiency requirements. These factors, combined with regulatory changes, have created a challenging environment for property investors.

Future Challenges for Landlords

Looking ahead, landlords face further regulatory and financial hurdles. From late 2026, the government plans to introduce a mandatory PRS Database, requiring landlords to register and pay an annual fee. Additionally, the introduction of a Landlord Ombudsman is expected in 2028, adding another layer of oversight. Tax changes are also on the horizon, with separate property income tax rates of 22%, 42%, and 47% set to take effect from April 2027.

Energy-efficiency standards present another significant cost for landlords. By 1 October 2030, privately rented homes must meet higher standards, unless exemptions apply. Estimates suggest landlords may need to spend up to £10,000 per property on qualifying improvements, with average costs projected at £5,400 for properties below the required standard. For owners of high-value rental properties in England, the proposed High Value Council Tax Surcharge could add further financial strain from April 2028.

The National Picture

TwentyEA’s data indicates that the PRS has lost 18.6% of its rental stock nationally since the start of the decade. In London, the figure stands at 14.2%. Whilst the capital has seen a slightly lower rate of decline compared to the national average, the overall trend underscores the growing pressures on the rental market. With regulatory and financial challenges continuing to mount, landlords may increasingly consider selling their properties, potentially reducing the availability of rental homes for tenants.

As the PRS evolves, both landlords and tenants face a changing landscape. For landlords, staying informed about forthcoming regulations and planning for potential costs could help navigate these challenges. Meanwhile, tenants may find themselves with fewer rental options, highlighting the need for balanced policies that support both parties in the UK’s housing market.

item.title: Property fall-throughs jump as cost of failed sales climbs
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent data reveals a concerning trend in the UK property market, with a notable rise in the number of property transactions falling through before completion. According to analysis by House Buyer Bureau, using data from TwentyCi, an estimated 71,959 sales collapsed in the second quarter of 2026. This marks a 6.6% increase compared to the previous quarter, highlighting ongoing challenges in the homebuying process. Whilst the figures remain lower than those recorded in the same period last year, the rise underscores the financial and emotional toll that failed transactions can have on buyers, sellers, and estate agents alike.

The Financial Impact of Fall-Throughs

Failed property transactions come with significant financial consequences. House Buyer Bureau estimates that fall-throughs cost buyers and sellers £257.9 million during the quarter, up from £239.7 million in the first three months of 2026. This £18 million increase reflects the growing financial burden associated with collapsed sales. The average cost of a failed transaction also rose to £3,584, representing a 0.9% increase from the previous quarter and a 2.8% rise compared to the same period in 2025.

For estate agents, the impact extends beyond the immediate loss of potential commission. A fall-through often means remarketing the property, restarting negotiations, and rebuilding broken chains, all of which can be time-consuming and uncertain. Traditional agents, who typically receive their fees upon completion, may face delayed or lost income, adding to the challenges of managing such scenarios.

The Broader Implications for Buyers and Sellers

For homeowners and buyers, a collapsed sale can be particularly stressful. Sellers may face wasted time, additional costs, and the uncertainty of having to relist their property. This can be especially disruptive if they have already made plans based on the assumption that their sale would complete. Buyers, too, may experience financial losses and the frustration of needing to restart their property search.

Chris Hodgkinson, Managing Director of House Buyer Bureau, commented on the findings: “Whilst the number of fall-throughs remains lower than last year’s levels, the latest increase highlights the fragility of the homebuying process. The rising average cost of failed transactions means that every collapse carries significant financial consequences for those involved.”

Despite the challenges, there is some positive news. The overall volume of fall-throughs is still below last year’s figures, suggesting that there may be opportunities to improve certainty in the transaction process. Hodgkinson added: “There is considerable scope to enhance the reliability of property transactions, which would benefit buyers, sellers, and agents alike.”

As the property market continues to navigate these complexities, homeowners may wish to explore ways to minimise the risk of fall-throughs, such as seeking professional advice and ensuring thorough preparation before entering the buying or selling process.
